paragraphs.source_en: Now, do you know who it was that explained this contradictory phenomenon and, after a thousand years, rescued our doubts from the dark abyss? It was that Greek philosopher, Aristotle himself, founder of the Peripatetic school, revered as a scholar ever since learning began. His explanation runs like this: hey, stop tapping that cake plate and listen properly. The prizes the Greeks received in athletic contests were far more valuable than the feats they performed. That is why such prizes could serve as a means of encouragement and as a reward. But what of knowledge itself? If one were to give something as payment for knowledge, it would have to be something far more precious than knowledge. But is there, in all the world, any treasure more precious than knowledge? Naturally there cannot be. If you give an inadequate reward, you merely damage the dignity of knowledge. They meant to heap chests of gold and silver as high as Mount Olympus and pour out all the wealth of Croesus as a fitting recompense for knowledge, but after much reflection they perceived that no riches could possibly match it. From that time on, they simply decided to give nothing at all. You can see clearly from this that piles of copper coins and gold and silver cannot rival knowledge. Now that we have acknowledged this principle, let us apply it to the matter before us. What, after all, is this fellow Kaneda? Is he not merely a banknote with a nose and eyes stuck onto it? To describe him in a pithy phrase, he is nothing more than a walking banknote. The daughter of a walking banknote can amount, at best, to no more than a walking cheque. But turn around and look at Kangetsu: he had the honor of graduating first from the highest seat of learning, and after graduation, without the slightest hint of weariness, he hangs from his formal haori a cord dating from the Choshu campaign and studies day and night the stability of acorns; not satisfied even with that, he is soon to publish a great thesis that will overwhelm Lord Kelvin. True, once while passing over Azumabashi he put on a failed performance of throwing himself into the river, but that was merely one of those impulsive acts common to hot-blooded young men, and it does nothing to impair his essential nature as a wholesaler of knowledge. If I were to judge Kangetsu by one of my own Meitei-style comparisons, he is a walking library, a twenty-eight-centimeter shell kneaded out of knowledge. When that shell, once the time is ripe, explodes in the academic world, just you watch. There is no doubt it will explode... At this point Meitei could not immediately find the adjective he claimed was in his own distinctive style, and seemed about to dwindle into an anticlimax, but at once he went on: even thousands upon tens of thousands of such walking cheques would be smashed to powder. That is why I say Kangetsu must never be matched with such an ill-suited woman. I will not consent to it. It would be like marrying the wisest elephant among all the beasts to the greediest little pig.

paragraphs.source_en: I do not think it is necessarily so. Mr. Suzuki answered helplessly. Having already spoken plenty of ill of Meitei, if he were now to mention Hanamichiyanagi as well, there was no telling what a lawless person like the master might blurt out. So he felt the best course was to parry Meitei's sharp point as vaguely as possible and prevent the matter from developing any further complications. Mr. Suzuki is a clever man. He knows well that in the present age unnecessary resistance is to be avoided wherever possible, and that useless quarrels are relics of the feudal era. The purpose of life lies not in disputes of the tongue, but in action. So long as matters proceed steadily according to one's own intentions, the purpose of life has been achieved. If matters can advance as one wishes without hardship, anxiety, or argument, then the purpose of life can be achieved in a truly blissful fashion. After graduation Mr. Suzuki succeeded by this creed, hung a gold watch by this creed, accepted the commission from Mr. and Mrs. Kaneda by this creed, and by the same creed neatly and successfully persuaded Kushami, so that the affair was nine-tenths accomplished; then, all at once, in burst Meitei, a vagrant not to be governed by ordinary rules and suspected of possessing psychological operations beyond those of common men, leaving Suzuki at a loss before such a scene. The inventor of this creed of bliss was the gentleman of Meiji; the practitioner of this creed is Mr. Suzuki Tojuro; and the one now finding himself in difficulty because of this creed is also Mr. Suzuki Tojuro.
